items.answer: Keep Tag when the organization already uses Slack and Claude Team or Enterprise, wants Anthropic-native execution, and accepts Tag's shared-context and governance model. Switch only for a specific platform, data, or workflow advantage.

items.question: What is the best voice dictation tool for AI agents?
items.answer: It depends on whether you need cross-app input, technical vocabulary, local or offline processing, host-native input, or document-centered work.

items.question: How is dictation different from voice mode?
items.answer: Dictation produces editable text, while voice mode is an interaction channel that may use dictation, an agent, or both.

items.question: Should I choose system-wide or built-in dictation?
items.answer: System-wide dictation spans applications; built-in dictation is simpler when work stays inside one supported host.

items.question: How should I test dictation accuracy?
items.answer: Use your own names, technical terms, punctuation, file references, and spoken commands, then measure correction time.

items.question: How should I evaluate dictation privacy?
items.answer: Check audio and transcript processing, retention, telemetry, account controls, and optional cloud post-processing.

items.question: Does on-device dictation mean every feature is local?
items.answer: Not necessarily. Formatting, language-model cleanup, sync, or optional modes may still use cloud services.

items.question: Do I need more than one dictation tool?
items.answer: Only when separate tools cover genuinely different job shapes rather than duplicating the same input layer.

items.question: Which metrics matter in a trial?
items.answer: Measure correction time, latency, application coverage, vocabulary handling, data path, reliability, and total cost.

items.question: Does a browser AI agent need my password to act as me?
items.answer: No. An authenticated browser session can already carry your authority, so session access must be treated as a credential.

items.question: What browser-agent permissions should I check?
items.answer: Check site scope, tab and host access, cookies, downloads, history, clipboard, local files, debugger access, and native messaging.

items.question: How can I reduce browser-agent access?
items.answer: Use a dedicated profile, per-site or runtime grants, least-privileged accounts, and no banking, payroll, identity-admin, or production-cloud sessions.

items.question: What is indirect prompt injection?
items.answer: It is untrusted page, email, file, image, or tool content that tries to redirect the agent away from the user’s goal.

items.question: Which browser-agent actions need human approval?
items.answer: Sending, publishing, purchasing, deleting, changing permissions, deploying, and other high-consequence actions should require confirmation at the final step.

items.question: What should a browser-agent audit trail record?
items.answer: Record the user, policy, model, version, goal, sources, pages, tool calls, approvals, data movement, errors, timestamps, and final state.

items.question: How should a company pilot a browser agent?
items.answer: Start with read-only low-risk tasks in a dedicated profile, run injection tests, verify stop and recovery paths, then expand one permission at a time.

items.question: What security evidence should an enterprise request?
items.answer: Request data-flow and subprocessor details, retention and training terms, permission documentation, security assessments, incident procedures, and exportable run records.

items.question: What is a browser AI agent?
items.answer: An agent that observes pages and uses browser actions within a specific profile, session, and permission boundary.

items.question: Can it use my signed-in websites?
items.answer: Only when the selected browser surface supports that session and the user account has permission.

items.question: What tasks fit best?
items.answer: Read-only research, structured extraction, comparison, drafts, and reversible low-impact writes.

items.question: What tasks need approval?
items.answer: Purchases, submissions, deletion, permission changes, external messages, and legal or financial commitments.

items.question: Why does browser context matter?
items.answer: Built-in, extension, and cloud browsers can have different profiles, cookies, files, and controls.

items.question: How should success be verified?
items.answer: Check visible page state and backend state, and save stable identifiers or receipts.

items.question: What are common failures?
items.answer: Stale pages, hidden state, authentication, CAPTCHAs, layout changes, partial writes, and prompt injection.

items.question: How do I test safely?
items.answer: Use a bounded task, test account, expected-state checklist, reversible writes, and recorded failures.

items.question: Do I need an agentic AI system?
items.answer: Only when the route cannot be fully specified in advance and the system must choose tools using environmental feedback.

items.question: Should I build, buy, or use a hybrid?
items.answer: Choose by required control, strategic differentiation, governance, integration, evaluation, total cost, and exit requirements.

items.question: Which responsibilities cannot be outsourced?
items.answer: Your organization still owns the purpose, acceptable risk, human role, and decision to continue or stop deployment.

items.question: How should I compare build and buy options?
items.answer: Run every option against the same acceptance suite and a representative workload.

items.question: What belongs in total cost of ownership?
items.answer: Include building or configuration, model and runtime use, review, failures, monitoring, support, and migration.

items.question: Does owning the code prevent vendor lock-in?
items.answer: No. Models, data schemas, tools, evaluations, and operational knowledge can still create lock-in.

items.question: What is a defensible hybrid architecture?
items.answer: Keep policy, evaluations, and data boundaries under your control while buying replaceable runtime or connector layers.

items.question: How should I test an exit path?
items.answer: Export configurations, data, and traces, then rehearse replacing one important dependency.

items.question: What is calendar-driven AI?
items.answer: It is an AI workflow whose eligibility and timing come from a dated event, deadline, or recurrence rule. The event can route context and start a bounded task without a fresh chat prompt.

items.question: How is calendar-driven AI different from chat-based AI?
items.answer: Chat starts when a person asks and supports evolving instructions. Calendar-driven work starts when a time rule is met and is better for stable recurring jobs with known sources, outputs, and exception owners.

items.question: Is scheduled AI automatically an AI agent?
items.answer: No. A scheduled reminder or fixed prompt may have no reasoning, tools, or recovery behavior. Agentic scheduling additionally requires context selection, bounded actions, observable failures, and an escalation path.

items.question: When should I use chat instead of a calendar trigger?
items.answer: Use chat for novel, ambiguous, sensitive, or judgment-heavy work where instructions change during execution and a person needs to inspect intermediate steps.

items.question: When is a calendar trigger the better choice?
items.answer: Use it when timing is part of the task specification, the job repeats, sources and output are stable, late or missing results are detectable, and someone owns exceptions.

items.question: What can go wrong with calendar-driven AI?
items.answer: Wrong eligibility rules, duplicate events, timezone changes, stale templates, revoked connectors, and silent repeat failures can compound. Every workflow needs run history, source logs, retry rules, and a pause control.

items.question: Can calendar-driven and chat-based AI work together?
items.answer: Yes. Let the calendar create a bounded draft, then let the user open a conversation to question, revise, or approve it. Confirmed results can return to the project or next event.

items.question: How should I calculate the cost of scheduled AI?
items.answer: Multiply eligible runs by retrieval, model, tool, and review cost, then compare that with time saved on artifacts people actually use. Track false triggers and unopened outputs, not only token price.

items.question: What is the difference between ChatGPT Voice Mode and dictation?
items.answer: Voice holds a spoken exchange; Dictation creates editable text before you send it.

items.question: Which is better for writing a precise prompt?
items.answer: Dictation, because you can inspect names, constraints, and formatting before submission.

items.question: Does Voice Mode leave an exact transcript?
items.answer: OpenAI warns that voice transcripts may not match the conversation exactly.

items.question: Does ChatGPT Dictation send automatically?
items.answer: Its documented flow is to transcribe, let you edit, and then send; verify current app behavior before relying on it.

items.question: Is Voice Mode better for brainstorming?
items.answer: Often, when rapid follow-up and spoken pacing matter more than a reusable prompt.

items.question: Which should I use for agent instructions?
items.answer: Prefer editable text for high-impact or repeatable instructions; use Voice to explore first if helpful.

items.question: Do Voice and Dictation have the same privacy controls?
items.answer: They are separate features; review OpenAI’s current data-control and retention documentation for each.

items.question: Can I combine both in one workflow?
items.answer: Yes. Explore aloud, then dictate or type a reviewed instruction into the composer.

items.question: Can non-developers use Claude Code?
items.answer: Yes, if they can work carefully in a terminal and review file changes; it is not a no-code app.

items.question: What can a solo operator do with Claude Code?
items.answer: They can draft, transform, and organize text or data files, automate repeatable repository tasks, and inspect changes.

items.question: Do I need to know Git to use Claude Code?
items.answer: Basic version control is strongly recommended because it makes changes inspectable and recoverable.

items.question: What should I not automate first?
items.answer: Avoid credentials, payments, destructive bulk edits, and legally sensitive decisions until controls are proven.

items.question: How much does Claude Code cost?
items.answer: It depends on the current plan, model, and workload; use Anthropic’s official pricing and a bounded pilot.

items.question: How should file permissions be scoped?
items.answer: Start in a copy or narrow project folder and expand only after reviewing behavior.

items.question: Is Cowork a better choice for non-coding work?
items.answer: It may offer a more suitable surface for document work; compare permissions, artifacts, and review flow.

items.question: What is a reproducible first Claude Code pilot?
items.answer: Give it one version-controlled folder, one reversible task, and an explicit acceptance checklist.

items.question: What is the main difference between Claude Code, Cowork, and Tag?
items.answer: Claude Code works from a repository, Cowork works across a person's files and connected apps, and Tag works in shared Slack context. Choose the surface that matches the task's source of truth and reviewer.

items.question: When should I use Claude Code?
items.answer: Use Claude Code when repository source, tests, diffs, and engineering review define whether the work is complete.

items.question: When should I use Claude Cowork?
items.answer: Use Cowork when one owner needs Claude to carry a multi-step knowledge-work task across documents, files, and approved connectors.

items.question: When should I use Claude Tag?
items.answer: Use Tag when the task belongs to a team channel and the useful context, review, and handoff should remain visible in Slack.

items.question: Is Claude Cowork still a separate mode?
items.answer: It depends on the current Claude app experience. Anthropic has been moving capabilities into a more unified Claude interface, so check the product surface available to your account rather than relying on an older label.

items.question: Can the three Claude surfaces be combined?
items.answer: Yes. A team can coordinate in Tag, do document-heavy preparation in Cowork, and hand repository changes to Claude Code, provided ownership and review stay explicit.

items.question: How do future or scheduled tasks differ across Cowork and Tag?
items.answer: Anthropic says Tag can plan future work and schedule tasks for itself after a person delegates in Slack. Cowork's cloud or scheduled work remains distinct from local-file access, which depends on an authorized desktop connection.

items.question: What is the safest way to adopt these Claude agents?
items.answer: Pilot one reversible workflow with limited permissions, a named reviewer, clear completion criteria, and an audit trail before expanding access.

items.question: What are Claude Managed Agents?
items.answer: They are Anthropic-hosted infrastructure for durable agent sessions, controlled tools, and observable execution.

items.question: Is a Managed Agent just Claude chat running for longer?
items.answer: No. It is a runtime and building layer for operating agents, not simply a longer chat mode.

items.question: Does a one-person company need Managed Agents?
items.answer: Only when a recurring workflow needs a service boundary, durable sessions, controlled tools, and operational visibility.

items.question: What infrastructure can Managed Agents replace?
items.answer: They may reduce work around sandboxes, session recovery, credential handling, and traces, but not process design or human review.

items.question: Which actions should remain human-approved?
items.answer: Messages, purchases, deletions, production changes, and other consequential external actions should require approval.

items.question: How should a solo operator pilot Managed Agents?
items.answer: Start with one reversible workflow, low-sensitivity data, minimal tool permissions, logging, and explicit failure tests.

items.question: How should I estimate Managed Agent cost?
items.answer: Include model usage, runtime, retries, storage, monitoring, and the time required to investigate failures.

items.question: Should I use a Managed Agent or an AI workspace?
items.answer: Use a workspace for supervised, judgment-heavy work and consider a managed runtime for service-like, repeatable execution.

items.question: What is the safest first step for an AI Downloads cleanup?
items.answer: Copy 20 to 50 representative files into a disposable test folder before touching the real Downloads folder.

items.question: Should an AI organizer delete files during the first run?
items.answer: No. Disable deletion and require a proposal or preview before any move or rename.

items.question: What should a Downloads cleanup instruction include?
items.answer: Define the outcome, destination folders, naming rules, exclusions, a no-delete rule, and a preview requirement.

items.question: How should I verify a proposed cleanup?
items.answer: Check ambiguous files, duplicate handling, filename collisions, destination paths, and files the tool could not classify.

items.question: Is undo guaranteed after a bulk file operation?
items.answer: No. Test the product’s documented recovery behavior on copies and do not assume an operating-system undo will work.

items.question: When should I enable a watched Downloads folder?
items.answer: Only after the same rules succeed repeatedly on representative samples and failure cases have been tested.

items.question: Which files should stay outside the first cleanup?
items.answer: Exclude sensitive, shared, synchronized, encrypted, application-managed, and legally retained files until their behavior is understood.

items.question: How often should I review Downloads?
items.answer: Choose a cadence based on file volume and ambiguity, then process only new files in small approved batches.

items.question: What is the core difference between Codex for Chrome and Claude for Chrome?
items.answer: Compare background delegation with sidebar collaboration using current official documentation.

items.question: Which is better for multi-tab work?
items.answer: Test the same task and record context loss, site switching, and approval steps.

items.question: Can either agent use signed-in sites?
items.answer: Only within documented permissions and the site access you explicitly grant.

items.question: How should browser-agent permissions be tested?
items.answer: Start with trusted, low-risk sites and the minimum scope needed for one task.

items.question: How should I handle prompt injection?
items.answer: Treat page content as untrusted and require approval for consequential actions.

items.question: Which plan is required?
items.answer: Verify current vendor pricing and extension documentation instead of relying on an old comparison table.

items.question: Can both extensions run together?
items.answer: They can be installed together, but avoid overlapping sensitive grants and track permissions separately.

items.question: What pilot should I run?
items.answer: Use one browsing task with the same sites, output, and acceptance rubric for both tools.

items.question: What is Codex Harness?
items.answer: It is the open agent runtime and integration layer behind Codex workflows.

items.question: Which components are open?
items.answer: OpenAI names Codex CLI, app-server, and the official SDK as open-source components.

items.question: Are model weights included?
items.answer: No. Model access and managed services remain separate.

items.question: When should I use codex exec?
items.answer: Use it for bounded scripts, CI jobs, and one-off background work.

items.question: When should I use the SDK?
items.answer: Use it when application code must start, resume, or stream tasks.

items.question: When should I use app-server?
items.answer: Use it when an agent is part of a persistent product UI with events, interruption, and approvals.

items.question: Does open source remove inference cost?
items.answer: No. Budget model access separately.

items.question: What must an embedding product still own?
items.answer: It still owns context, tools, permissions, approval UX, observability, and system-of-record writes.

items.question: What is context engineering for AI agents?
items.answer: It is the design of the instructions, tools, retrieved evidence, task state, environment data, and memory available when an agent makes a decision.

items.question: How is context engineering different from prompt engineering?
items.answer: Prompt engineering focuses on how a request is expressed. Context engineering also decides which evidence and tools are available, how permissions apply, what persists, and how state is compacted across a multi-step run.

items.question: Does a larger context window always improve an agent?
items.answer: No. Stale plans, similar records, overlapping tools, and untrusted instructions can crowd out relevant evidence. The goal is decision-relevant precision, not maximum token volume.

items.question: What belongs in an agent's context?
items.answer: Include stable policy, current task state, clear tool contracts, minimal authoritative evidence, temporary working memory, and only the durable memories whose provenance and lifecycle are defined.

items.question: How should an agent handle retrieved documents?
items.answer: Treat retrieved text as data, preserve source and timestamp, filter by identity and permissions, rank authoritative records first, expose conflicts, and prevent document instructions from overriding system policy.

items.question: What is context compaction?
items.answer: It is the replacement of long histories with smaller structured state. Good compaction preserves decisions, commitments, owners, deadlines, evidence links, attempted actions, and unresolved conflicts.

items.question: What should become durable agent memory?
items.answer: Persist only information that remains useful across sessions and has an owner, provenance, confirmation rule, expiry or review date, and deletion path. Temporary hypotheses should expire with the task.

items.question: How do I evaluate context engineering?
items.answer: Test missing, stale, conflicting, malicious, and permission-restricted inputs. Measure source precision, missing evidence, unauthorized retrieval, unsupported claims, tool-selection errors, recovery, and context cost per accepted task.

items.question: What is Cordis?
items.answer: Cordis is the vendored framework DeepSeek Harness uses to compose plugins, contexts, services, dependency injection, effects, and events.

items.question: Why does DeepSeek Harness use Cordis?
items.answer: Cordis gives Harness replaceable modules and explicit lifecycle control, so tools and services can be mounted, waited on, reloaded, and cleaned up predictably.

items.question: What is a Cordis Context?
items.answer: A Context is the container through which a plugin accesses services, registers behavior, and scopes resources to a lifecycle.

items.question: How does dependency injection work in Cordis?
items.answer: Plugins declare the services they require with injection rules. Cordis waits for those services and activates or deactivates dependent behavior as availability changes.

items.question: What are reversible effects in Cordis?
items.answer: Effects pair a side effect with a disposer. When a plugin unloads or its context ends, Cordis runs cleanup so listeners, timers, and other resources do not leak.

items.question: Does Cordis support hot reload?
items.answer: Its lifecycle and reversible-effect design support safe plugin reload patterns, provided the plugin registers its resources through the framework's cleanup mechanisms.

items.question: Is Cordis an agent model or a security sandbox?
items.answer: No. Cordis is runtime composition infrastructure. It does not supply an AI model and does not replace operating-system isolation, permission design, or application-level security controls.

items.question: When should a Harness extension become a Cordis plugin?
items.answer: Use a plugin when the extension has an independent lifecycle, depends on shared services, or must be removable and testable without rewriting the main runtime.

items.question: Do I actually need custom AI agent development?
items.answer: Only if a validated task needs model-directed decisions and existing products cannot meet the integration, permission, or deployment boundary. If fixed rules can describe the path, use deterministic automation. If the workflow is still unclear, prototype before commissioning a production agent.

items.question: What belongs in a custom agent requirements contract?
items.answer: Define the trigger, allowed inputs, required outcome, non-goals, model decisions, tools, approval points, refusal and escalation rules, acceptance tests, and behavior during timeout, partial completion, duplicate events, or outages. Include forbidden actions as well as desired features.

items.question: What architecture does a production AI agent need?
items.answer: At minimum: a task interface, orchestration harness, versioned model policy, narrow tools, explicit state, authorization and approval policies, evaluation and observability, plus a controlled execution boundary. A framework name alone is not an architecture.

items.question: How should tools and permissions be designed?
items.answer: Give each tool one clear purpose, a precise schema, minimum access, server-side validation, bounded retries, and idempotency for writes. Separate read, draft, reversible write, external action, and irreversible action. Require explicit approval or separate authorization for consequential operations.

items.question: How do you evaluate a custom AI agent?
items.answer: Use versioned tasks covering normal work, ambiguity, tool failure, duplicate events, prompt injection, required approvals, refusals, and previous incidents. Grade the final state, execution trace, unauthorized actions, intervention, latency, cost, and recovery—not only the text response.

items.question: What must be included in the final delivery?
items.answer: Require the task contract, architecture and data-flow diagrams, tool and state specifications, permission matrix, threat model, versioned eval suite, acceptance report, reproducible deployment, monitoring, rollback and incident runbooks, source and IP terms, credentials transfer, and owner training.

items.question: Should I build, buy, or use a hybrid?
items.answer: Buy or configure for standard workflows, build when a proprietary process or control boundary justifies operational ownership, and use a hybrid when only one layer is distinctive. Custom does not have to mean rebuilding identity, model access, scheduling, and observability from scratch.

items.question: How is this guide different from the AI agent development services article?
items.answer: This guide defines the system to build and the technical evidence required for acceptance. The services article covers sourcing: comparing agencies or freelancers, structuring a paid pilot and contract, reviewing pricing structure, and managing the provider relationship.

items.question: What is DeepSeek function calling?
items.answer: It is a model request for your application to execute a structured tool.

items.question: Does the model execute tools itself?
items.answer: No. Your code validates, authorizes, executes, and returns results.

items.question: What model name should new examples use?
items.answer: Use current documented names such as deepseek-flash and verify the live catalog.

items.question: What is strict mode for?
items.answer: It can improve schema adherence where supported, but business validation is still required.

items.question: Can calls run in parallel?
items.answer: A model may return multiple calls, but the executor must cap safe concurrency.

items.question: How should tool errors be returned?
items.answer: Return bounded structured results that let the loop stop, retry, or request review.

items.question: When is MCP useful?
items.answer: Use it when tools need standardized discovery or isolated credentials. MCP is implemented by the client or harness; the model still emits tool calls.

items.question: Is reasoning_content an audit record?
items.answer: No. Treat it as a protocol or debugging field, not a reliable explanation of a decision or evidence for approval.

items.question: Is DeepSeek Agent a direct alternative to Claude Code?
items.answer: Not exactly. Claude Code is a harness; DeepSeek usually supplies the model endpoint, and DeepSeek officially documents using that endpoint inside Claude Code.

items.question: Can Claude Code use DeepSeek models?
items.answer: Yes. DeepSeek documents an Anthropic-compatible base URL and the required Claude Code environment variables.

items.question: Does a DeepSeek endpoint preserve every Claude Code feature?
items.answer: Do not assume parity; test tools, caching, thinking, search, images, errors, and model mappings.

items.question: Which option is cheaper?
items.answer: DeepSeek publishes lower token rates, but compare total cost per accepted task, including retries and tools.

items.question: Is deepseek-v4-pro always served by V4 Pro?
items.answer: Not currently guaranteed. DeepSeek announced temporary routing to V4.1 Flash while V4.1-Pro is pending.

items.question: Should public coding benchmarks decide the winner?
items.answer: No. Harnesses, prompts, tools, and scoring differ; use repository-specific acceptance tests.

items.question: When should a team keep native Claude Code?
items.answer: Keep it when vendor-supported behavior and the Claude model stack matter more than the minimum token price.

items.question: What is the safest way to test DeepSeek routing?
items.answer: Start with reversible tasks, keep harness settings fixed, log failures, and require review before merge.

items.question: Is DeepSeek V4.1 Flash still a beta?
items.answer: No. It is the production Flash model served as deepseek-flash.

items.question: What happened to the expiring beta ID?
items.answer: It expired and should not be used in production configuration.

items.question: Are deepseek-v4-flash aliases still the old model?
items.answer: No. DeepSeek says the old models are retired and legacy aliases route to V4.1 Flash.

items.question: Does V4.1 Flash support images?
items.answer: Yes. The official model table lists vision support.

items.question: What are its context and output limits?
items.answer: The current table lists 1M context and up to 384K output.

items.question: How does peak pricing work?
items.answer: Weekday peak windows cost twice the published off-peak rates; check the live pricing page.

items.question: Is V4.1 Flash universally better than V4 Pro?
items.answer: Vendor results support the release claim, but workload-specific tests are still required.

items.question: What should teams retest during migration?
items.answer: Retest vision, tool calls, structured output, reasoning modes, caching, retries, and model logging.

items.question: Which DeepSeek API model should a solo operator start with?
items.answer: Start with deepseek-flash on a reversible task, then escalate only if evaluations justify it.

items.question: What are the current Flash prices?
items.answer: Cache-miss input is $0.15/$0.30 and output is $0.60/$1.20 per million tokens off-peak/peak.

items.question: Why is token price not the full budget?
items.answer: Retries, tools, storage, monitoring, and rejected outputs add cost.

items.question: How should cost be compared?
items.answer: Divide all run costs by the number of outputs that pass human acceptance.

items.question: When does prompt caching help?
items.answer: It helps when stable prefixes repeat; measure real hit rates instead of padding prompts.

items.question: What controls belong in a pilot?
items.answer: Use weekly caps, per-task call limits, logs, idempotency, and approval before external writes.

items.question: Is a rolling model alias suitable for regulated work?
items.answer: It may not be; ask for a pinned option when checkpoint identity is required.

items.question: What should the acceptance set include?
items.answer: Include ordinary, long-context, malformed, missing-evidence, duplicate, and approval-required cases.

items.question: Is DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 a new model or an update?
items.answer: It is the production build of V4 Pro, the same architecture as the April preview (1.6T-parameter MoE, 49B active, 1M context) with updated post-training. DeepSeek swapped the deepseek-v4-pro endpoint to this checkpoint on August 12–13, 2026; no integration change is required.

items.question: How do I access DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813?
items.answer: Use the existing deepseek-v4-pro model name on the DeepSeek API. It is OpenAI- and Anthropic-format compatible, so existing integrations, including Claude Code pointed at [api.deepseek.com](<http://api.deepseek.com>), work without modification.

items.question: Are the 0813 benchmark scores independently verified?
items.answer: Not yet. All agent benchmark scores (DeepSWE 62.7, Terminal-Bench 2.1 87.9, Cybergym 83.3, and others) are vendor-reported and were produced through DeepSeek's unreleased Harness minimal mode. Independent trackers had recorded no third-party 0813 results at the time of writing.

items.question: When does the DeepSeek price increase take effect?
items.answer: August 16, 2026 at 16:00 UTC. Peak/off-peak billing starts then, with peak hours at 01:00–04:00 and 06:00–10:00 UTC and off-peak priced at half of peak. Peak V4 Pro output rises to $3.96 per 1M tokens, up from the current $0.87 flat rate.

items.question: Does DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 support images?
items.answer: No. This build is text-only. It accepts text input and produces text output; it does not natively support image, audio, or video input, despite some coverage suggesting otherwise.

items.question: Is DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 open-source?
items.answer: The V4 series weights are MIT-licensed, but the 0813 build's weights had not been published at the time of writing — Hugging Face still hosted the April preview build. The API is the guaranteed way to access 0813.

items.question: Do AI file organizers upload your files?
items.answer: Some do, some do not, and one app may differ by mode. Check whether names, text or page images leave the device.

items.question: What is the difference between local, BYOK and managed cloud?
items.answer: Local runs on-device; BYOK sends data to your chosen provider; managed cloud uses infrastructure selected by the app vendor.

items.question: Does not stored mean not uploaded?
items.answer: No. Data can be transmitted, processed and deleted without long-term storage. Ask separately about transmission, logs and retention.

items.question: Does BYOK keep files private?
items.answer: It may bypass the app vendor, but data still reaches the model provider unless the endpoint is local.

items.question: Can an offline test prove nothing is uploaded?
items.answer: No. It shows a feature can run locally in that configuration, not what happens online. Add network logs and policy review.

items.question: What should I look for in a privacy policy?
items.answer: Check transmitted data, location, subprocessors, retention, training use, deletion and mode-specific terms.

items.question: Is local processing automatically secure or compliant?
items.answer: No. It reduces transfer but leaves device encryption, access, backups and policy to you.

items.question: What is the safest evaluation method?
items.answer: Start with synthetic files, select the mode, review disclosures, record network behavior, then test noncritical copies.

items.question: What are Dynamic Workflows?
items.answer: Anthropic describes generated orchestration code that delegates work to subagents and consolidates results.

items.question: When should I build orchestration?
items.answer: When a repeated task needs explicit decomposition, specialized roles, custom validation, and owned execution order.

items.question: When should I use a workspace?
items.answer: When changing inputs, artifacts, human steering, connected tools, and review matter more than custom coordination.

items.question: Is more agents always better?
items.answer: No. Compare against a single-agent baseline and measure quality, latency, and cost.

items.question: Can a workspace run workflows?
items.answer: It may, depending on the product; workspace and orchestration are overlapping layers.

items.question: What must a build owner maintain?
items.answer: Code, tools, permissions, evaluations, observability, cost controls, upgrades, and recovery.

items.question: What should a pilot include?
items.answer: One bounded task, rubric, baseline, capped tools, time, and spend, plus failure tests.

items.question: What is the deciding trade-off?
items.answer: Custom control versus operational ownership.

items.question: What is AI effort control?
items.answer: It adjusts how much reasoning a supported model applies, trading thoroughness against latency and token use.

items.question: Is Fast Mode the same as lower effort?
items.answer: No. Effort changes reasoning depth; Fast Mode changes serving speed on supported models, usually at premium pricing.

items.question: Which tasks should use low effort?
items.answer: Extraction, formatting, classification, and other reversible tasks with deterministic checks are good starting points.

items.question: When should I increase effort?
items.answer: Increase it for competing constraints, difficult diagnosis, long plans, or costly mistakes after a lower setting fails a named acceptance criterion.

items.question: When is Fast Mode worth the premium?
items.answer: Use it when waiting blocks a person or dependent step and the saved time has measurable value.

items.question: Should important work always use maximum effort?
items.answer: No. Importance and reasoning difficulty differ; maximum effort can add cost without improving accepted output.

items.question: How do I test effort levels fairly?
items.answer: Run representative tasks at standard speed, score accepted results and reviewer time, then test Fast Mode on the winning effort level.

items.question: What should I measure besides latency?
items.answer: Measure total time to acceptance, cost, corrections, constraint failures, reviewer minutes, and whether the output was used.

items.question: Do I need an enterprise Feishu account to use the Feishu CLI?
items.answer: Yes, effectively. The open platform features the CLI wraps aren't fully available on personal free accounts, and building anything real requires creating a custom app in the developer console — which needs an account with app-creation permissions. If you run your own workspace, you typically have them, but verify before you invest time in setup.

items.question: What's the difference between a bot token and a user access token?
items.answer: A bot or tenant token lets the app act as itself — fine for chats the bot is in and documents shared with the app. A user access token lets the CLI act on your behalf, which is required for private chats, personal calendars, and anything not explicitly shared with the app — meaning most of your real working conversations need it. It also brings the token refresh burden.

items.question: How often do user access tokens expire and break automated workflows?
items.answer: Often enough that expiry is the classic silent killer: user access tokens typically last around two hours and need a refresh mechanism to keep automated flows alive. If you don't touch a setup for a few weeks, you'll come back to find everything quietly failing — with no alert, because you never built an alerting layer. Plan refresh or re-authentication up front.

items.question: Can I run Feishu CLI workflows on a schedule without a server?
items.answer: Locally, yes — cron on Mac/Linux or Task Scheduler on Windows covers many cases. But the CLI only runs when invoked, so any external trigger needs something in the middle: a cron job, a script runner, or a small automation layer. Workflows that must run while your machine is off need an always-on environment such as a cheap VPS — small, but real infrastructure.

items.question: What happens when Feishu updates or deprecates an API I'm using?
items.answer: Feishu announces deprecations with migration windows, but as a solo operator you'll usually find out when a workflow silently fails or returns unexpected results — there's no mailing list, QA environment, or test suite to catch it first. The realistic mitigation is unglamorous: keep the CLI and dependencies updated, watch the platform changelog, and make failures loud.

items.question: When does Feishu CLI automation actually pay off for a solo operator?
items.answer: It pays off when the workflow runs frequently, the manual version is genuinely tedious, and the failure mode is low-stakes — read-only pipelines that pull context for your own reference are the best starting point. Action-execution workflows that send messages or modify shared records carry more risk, so graduate to them later. You should also enjoy the meta-work of maintaining it.

items.question: Is Lark CLI an official tool?
items.answer: Yes. The larksuite team maintains the official Lark/Feishu CLI repository.

items.question: What is the safest first automation?
items.answer: Start with a read-only retrieval task, log every command, and add write scopes only with an owner and rollback.

items.question: What is the difference between an organizer, sorter and renamer?
items.answer: A sorter routes, a renamer changes names, and an organizer combines content understanding with naming and placement.

items.question: What if my folders are already correct?
items.answer: Choose a renamer to improve searchability without redesigning the tree.

items.question: What if names are clear but files are misplaced?
items.answer: Choose a sorter, often deterministic rules. AI is unnecessary when surface signals reveal the destination.

items.question: When do I need a full organizer?
items.answer: When names and structure are poor and correct filing depends on information inside each file.

items.question: Is a sorter the same as a rules engine?
items.answer: Not always. Some infer categories with AI; rules are preferable when routing logic can be written precisely.

items.question: Can one product be all three?
items.answer: Yes. Check the default mode, what each mode reads, and whether moves are previewed and reversible.

items.question: Which category is safest?
items.answer: None inherently. Use copies, preview batches, test recovery and keep an independent backup.

items.question: Can I combine a sorter and an organizer?
items.answer: Yes. Use rules for obvious recurring files and content-aware organizing for ambiguous leftovers.

items.question: What should count as a customer?
items.answer: Choose paid accounts, completed transactions, active subscribers, or a retained cohort and use the definition consistently.

items.question: How should a solo founder get customers zero through ten?
items.answer: Focus on one buyer and problem, use legitimate direct contact, and offer a bounded paid pilot.

items.question: Why charge early?
items.answer: A paid offer tests willingness to pay rather than usage or polite interest alone.

items.question: What should I learn from customers ten through thirty?
items.answer: Record buying reasons, onboarding friction, time to first value, support, retention, and loss reasons.

items.question: What should be standardized between customers thirty and one hundred?
items.answer: Standardize only repeated qualification, proposal, onboarding, education, and feedback steps.

items.question: Should early customer outreach be automated?
items.answer: Not until the message earns replies and platform, privacy, and reputation risks are controlled.

items.question: Which customer metrics should I review weekly?
items.answer: Track qualified conversations, offers, paid conversions, first value, retention, support, refunds, and loss reasons.

items.question: What should the first 100 customers leave behind?
items.answer: They should clarify the ideal customer, promise, price, onboarding, acquisition channel, and support load.

items.question: Is FloatCup still a live World Cup calendar?
items.answer: No. The tournament ended July 19, 2026, and this page now treats FloatCup as a historical archive.
