items.answer: The completed tournament contained 104 matches.

items.question: Are FloatCup results authoritative?
items.answer: No. Use FIFA’s official fixtures and results page as the sporting source of truth.

items.question: Why keep the calendar?
items.answer: Keep it only if a dated tournament record is useful for research or personal history.

items.question: Why remove the calendar?
items.answer: Remove it if 104 completed events make calendar search or navigation noisy.

items.question: How should I remove it?
items.answer: Use the calendar-level unsubscribe or remove action in the client where it was added.

items.question: Will the archive receive live reminders?
items.answer: No current reminders or live schedule updates are promised after the completed tournament.

items.question: Is Gemini 3.5 Flash still available?
items.answer: Yes. `gemini-3.5-flash` remains a stable Gemini API model, but Google's current catalog labels it a legacy Flash model. New projects should compare it with Google's current recommended Flash models instead of assuming 3.5 is still the default choice.

items.question: What are Gemini 3.5 Flash's context and output limits?
items.answer: Google documents a 1,048,576-token input limit and a 65,536-token maximum output. It accepts text, images, video, audio, and PDFs, but produces text rather than native images or audio.

items.question: How much does the Gemini 3.5 Flash API cost?
items.answer: Google currently lists standard paid pricing at $1.50 per million input tokens and $9 per million output tokens, including thinking tokens. Batch is $0.75 input and $4.50 output; caching and Search or Maps grounding add separate charges. Check the live pricing page before budgeting.

items.question: Can I upload confidential client files to Gemini 3.5 Flash?
items.answer: Do not send confidential or personal information through unpaid Gemini API or AI Studio services; Google's terms say unpaid content may be used for product improvement and human review. Paid API and qualifying Workspace accounts have different protections, but you must still verify retention, permissions, and any enabled grounding or logging features.

items.question: Can Gemini 3.5 Flash analyze a long PDF in one request?
items.answer: It can accept PDFs within its context and file limits, but capacity does not guarantee perfect recall. Test several document lengths, require file and page citations, and sample claims whose evidence appears at the beginning, middle, and end.

items.question: Which tools does Gemini 3.5 Flash support?
items.answer: It supports function calling, code execution, file search, URL context, Google Search and Maps grounding, structured output, caching, and Batch API. Computer Use is preview; Live API, native image generation, and audio generation are not supported.

items.question: Should a new project use Gemini 3.5 Flash or a newer Gemini model?
items.answer: Evaluate the current recommended model first. Keep 3.5 when an existing integration is validated and migration offers little benefit; for a new build, compare current quality, latency, tool support, and total cost on the same representative task set.

items.question: How should a solo operator test a Gemini integration?
items.answer: Choose one weekly task, collect 20–30 representative cases, define accuracy and citation thresholds, run the current workflow as a baseline, then compare total cost and review time. Keep actions read-only until errors, duplicate calls, and partial failures are understood.

items.question: What is the exact Gemini 3.7 Flash model ID?
items.answer: The Developer API identifier is `gemini-3.7-flash`.

items.question: How large is its context window?
items.answer: Google lists 1,048,576 input tokens and up to 65,536 output tokens.

items.question: What does Gemini 3.7 Flash cost?
items.answer: Through December 31, 2026, Google lists $0.75/MTok input and $3.75/MTok output on the standard paid tier; the listed rates double January 1, 2027.

items.question: Which inputs and tools does it support?
items.answer: It accepts text, image, audio, and video inputs and supports agent features such as function calling; verify the endpoint and region for each tool.

items.question: How do I migrate from an older Flash model?
items.answer: Replay real requests, replace legacy thinking parameters with `thinking_level`, remove rejected fields, canary writes, and retain rollback.

items.question: Is Gemini 3.7 Flash obsolete after 3.8?
items.answer: No. It remains useful where accepted-task quality is stable and predictable latency or tokens matter more than persistent reasoning.

items.question: How should I compare 3.7 with 3.8?
items.answer: Compare accepted-task cost, p95 latency, tool recovery, and correction time on the same workload.

items.question: What is the biggest pricing trap?
items.answer: Thinking output, cache storage, grounding, retries, and endpoint class can matter more than the headline input rate.

items.question: What is the Gemini 3.8 Flash model ID?
items.answer: Use `gemini-3.8-flash`.

items.question: What changed from 3.7?
items.answer: Google emphasizes longer-horizon planning, iterative tools, and verification; that can improve completion while using more tokens.

items.question: Which thinking levels are supported?
items.answer: Low, medium, and high are supported; medium is default and minimal is not accepted.

items.question: What are its context limits?
items.answer: Google lists 1,048,576 input tokens and up to 65,536 output tokens.

items.question: How much does it cost?
items.answer: The official standard paid rate through December 31, 2026 is $0.75/MTok input and $3.75/MTok output, including thinking.

items.question: Is Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber the same endpoint?
items.answer: No. The Cyber variant has separate access and claims that should not be transferred to the general model.

items.question: When should I keep Gemini 3.7?
items.answer: Keep 3.7 when it already passes routine tasks and wins on p95 latency or accepted-task cost.

items.question: What should a 3.8 pilot measure?
items.answer: Measure completion, tool validity, wall time, total tokens, retries, and human correction at low and medium effort.

items.question: How does Genspark pricing work?
items.answer: Plans combine product access with credit-metered work; verify the current official rules.

items.question: How many credits does one task cost?
items.answer: Measure the balance before and after a representative output that passes review.

items.question: Do Genspark credits roll over?
items.answer: Check the current membership terms and do not assume unused value carries forward.

items.question: Is the free tier enough?
items.answer: It is enough only if your representative pilot completes within its current limits.

items.question: Which Genspark plan should I choose?
items.answer: Choose the smallest current tier that covers measured monthly volume plus retry headroom.

items.question: Are zero-credit features permanent?
items.answer: Treat them as current terms or promotions, not permanent promises.

items.question: What hidden costs should I include?
items.answer: Include review, retries, export cleanup, storage, administration, and failed runs.

items.question: How should teams evaluate Genspark pricing?
items.answer: Include seats, governance, ownership, and accepted outputs per month.

items.question: What is Genspark Super Agent?
items.answer: It is a workspace agent that coordinates tools and output surfaces for multi-step tasks.

items.question: Is Genspark Super Agent a chatbot?
items.answer: No; evaluate it by plans, actions, and artifacts rather than conversation alone.

items.question: What is a Sparkpage?
items.answer: It is a research-oriented output surface whose current behavior should be verified in official documentation.

items.question: Can Genspark create slides and sheets?
items.answer: Check the current official workspace documentation and supported export formats.

items.question: Can Genspark take real-world actions?
items.answer: Some documented tools can; test availability, permissions, and approval in a bounded pilot.

items.question: How is a Super Agent different from a chatbot?
items.answer: It coordinates multiple steps and artifacts instead of only returning a reply.

items.question: What should a Genspark pilot measure?
items.answer: Measure source quality, accepted output, retries, permissions, and credits consumed.

items.question: Where should I check Genspark pricing?
items.answer: Use the official pricing and membership pages at purchase time.

items.question: What is the main difference between Genspark and Manus?
items.answer: Genspark is a stronger starting candidate for research-to-artifact work, while Manus is a stronger candidate for broader multi-tool delegation; both claims require testing.

items.question: Which is better for research?
items.answer: Choose the product that returns inspectable sources, handles conflicting evidence, and performs reliably on your own corpus.

items.question: Which one creates better artifacts?
items.answer: Compare editability, source provenance, constraint retention, and cleanup time rather than judging screenshots alone.

items.question: Which agent is more autonomous?
items.answer: Autonomy varies by task, plan, integration, and permission level, and greater autonomy does not guarantee better results.

items.question: How should I compare Genspark and Manus fairly?
items.answer: Run the same bounded seven-task trial twice and record accuracy, interventions, cleanup, repeatability, and cost.

items.question: Which is cheaper, Genspark or Manus?
items.answer: The answer depends on current plans, credits, retries, premium tool calls, and your monthly workload.

items.question: Are Genspark and Manus safe for logged-in accounts?
items.answer: Only when permissions are narrowly scoped, consequential actions require approval, and writes can be inspected or reversed.

items.question: What should I do if neither product passes the test?
items.answer: Reduce the workflow scope or evaluate alternatives using the same evidence, permission, reliability, and cost criteria.

items.question: What is the GLM-5.3 API model ID?
items.answer: The hosted Z.ai identifier is `glm-5.3`.

items.question: Can GLM-5.3 disable thinking?
items.answer: No. Z.ai documents thinking as always enabled with low, high, or max reasoning effort.

items.question: How can I use GLM-5.3?
items.answer: Choose the hosted API, GLM Coding Plan in supported coding agents, or a verified open-weight deployment.

items.question: Are the weights open source?
items.answer: Verify the current artifact and GLM-specific license; open weights do not automatically mean OSI-approved open source.

items.question: What must I change when migrating?
items.answer: Remove `thinking.type: disabled`, validate reasoning events, tool JSON, streaming, cancellation, and token accounting.

items.question: Is it mainly a coding model?
items.answer: Z.ai positions it around long-horizon coding, but vendor benchmarks should become hypotheses for your own repository suite.

items.question: How should I compare API and self-hosting cost?
items.answer: Compare hosted tokens and retries with accelerators, idle capacity, replicas, observability, and operator labor.

items.question: Which route is best for a pilot?
items.answer: The hosted API is simplest; use Coding Plan for seat-based coding and weights only when control justifies operations and legal review.

items.question: Which is better, Google Calendar or Apple Calendar?
items.answer: Google usually fits cross-platform work and Workspace collaboration; iCloud Calendar fits Apple-centered personal or family use.

items.question: Can Apple Calendar display Google Calendar?
items.answer: Yes. Apple Calendar can act as a client for a Google account on Apple devices.

items.question: Should I maintain editable copies in both systems?
items.answer: No. Pick one source of truth and use account connection or subscription for the other view.

items.question: Is an ICS subscription two-way sync?
items.answer: Usually not. A subscribed feed is commonly read-only and may refresh with delay.

items.question: Which is better for sharing?
items.answer: It depends on collaborators and account policy. Google offers documented sharing roles, while iCloud sharing works best inside the Apple account context.

items.question: Which is better offline?
items.answer: Test the exact device and account combination; offline behavior differs between native apps, web access, and cached data.

items.question: How do I migrate safely?
items.answer: Export a backup, import into separate destination calendars, rebuild sharing and integrations, and test recurring exceptions before retiring the old source.

items.question: Does choosing Google mean giving up Apple’s app?
items.answer: No. You can keep Google as the account source while using Apple Calendar as the interface.

items.question: Should a Google Workspace company use Google Calendar?
items.answer: Usually yes, because identity, Meet, groups, resources, and administration stay in one ecosystem, subject to policy.

items.question: When is Outlook Calendar the better fit?
items.answer: When Exchange, Teams, shared mailboxes, room resources, delegation, and Microsoft 365 governance are central.

items.question: Can Google Calendar and Outlook sync perfectly?
items.answer: Do not assume it. Subscriptions and connectors can have delays or omit organizer, response, attachment, or status details.

items.question: What is the safest coexistence pattern?
items.answer: Keep one authoritative calendar per identity, expose only required availability, and use a unified view without duplicating ownership.

items.question: Which has better delegation?
items.answer: Compare the exact Workspace and Exchange roles your organization needs; sharing and delegate access are not interchangeable.

items.question: Which is better for room booking?
items.answer: Use the ecosystem that owns the organization’s resource accounts and test cross-tenant behavior.

items.question: How should tasks affect the choice?
items.answer: Google Calendar connects with Google Tasks; Outlook sits in a broader Microsoft task ecosystem. Test assignment, visibility, and mobile behavior.

items.question: What must be tested before migration?
items.answer: Test recurrence, organizers, attendee responses, time zones, attachments, privacy, rooms, tasks, and automations.

items.question: Are GPT-5.6 models available in Floatboat's default picker?
items.answer: No. GPT-5.6 Sol and Terra are configured in Floatboat's underlying evaluation and capacity layer, but they are not exposed in the default client picker.

items.question: Which GPT-5.6 models are configured below the picker?
items.answer: The confirmed matrix includes gpt-5.6-sol and gpt-5.6-terra below the picker. GPT-5.6 Luna is not in the confirmed matrix.

items.question: What is GPT-5.6 Sol designed for?
items.answer: OpenAI positions Sol for demanding reasoning and agentic work. That does not mean it is currently selectable in Floatboat.

items.question: What is GPT-5.6 Terra designed for?
items.answer: Terra is the lower-cost GPT-5.6 variant. In Floatboat, it is underlying configuration rather than a default-picker launch.

items.question: Is GPT-5.6 Luna supported by Floatboat?
items.answer: No confirmed Floatboat configuration lists GPT-5.6 Luna.

items.question: Do OpenAI's GPT-5.6 prices apply directly to Floatboat?
items.answer: Not necessarily. OpenAI's prices describe its own channels; Floatboat packaging and billing must be verified separately.

items.question: Is OpenAI access the same as Floatboat support?
items.answer: No. A model can exist in OpenAI's products while remaining below Floatboat's picker or absent from Floatboat.

items.question: What would confirm a Floatboat launch?
items.answer: The client picker or official Floatboat release documentation, not capacity configuration alone.

items.question: What are the three GPT-5.6 tiers?
items.answer: Sol is the high-capability tier, Terra balances cost and intelligence, and Luna targets focused high-volume work.

items.question: What are the current API prices?
items.answer: Sol is $4/$20, Terra $2/$12, and Luna $0.20/$1.20 per million input/output tokens.

items.question: Why do older articles show different prices?
items.answer: The June preview prices were later reduced in July and August.

items.question: Which GPT-5.6 model should be the default?
items.answer: Terra is the balanced starting point; validate it against your workload.

items.question: When should a workflow use Sol?
items.answer: Use it when a matched evaluation shows enough quality or retry reduction to justify the premium.

items.question: What is Luna best suited to?
items.answer: It fits narrow, high-volume tasks such as routing, classification, and first-pass extraction.

items.question: How are prompts over 272K priced?
items.answer: Current model pages apply 2x input and 1.5x output rates to the full request.

items.question: Should new projects still start with GPT-5.6?
items.answer: Compare current GPT-6 tiers too; retain GPT-5.6 when matched evaluations support it.

items.question: What is GPT-6 Astra?
items.answer: It is OpenAI’s highest-capability API model for demanding reasoning, coding, computer use, research, and documents.

items.question: What does Astra cost?
items.answer: Standard text pricing is $10 input, $1 cached input, and $50 output per million tokens; cache writes are $12.50.

items.question: What are its context and output limits?
items.answer: It has a 1.05M context window and 128K maximum output.

items.question: What happens above 272K input tokens?
items.answer: The full request uses 2x input/cache and 1.5x output rates.

items.question: Which tools does Astra support?
items.answer: The Responses API lists search, code interpreter, hosted shell, computer use, MCP, skills, and other tools, subject to access controls.

items.question: What does Critical cyber capability mean for users?
items.answer: Astra has stronger safeguards; advanced requests may be refused and some defensive access is vetted through Daybreak.

items.question: Should benchmark scores determine adoption?
items.answer: No. Test the model, harness, reasoning setting, tools, and policy controls together.

items.question: When is Astra worth using?
items.answer: Use it when higher acceptance or fewer retries offsets its premium; cheaper GPT-6 tiers fit routine volume better.

items.question: What can GPT Image 2 do in a comic workflow?
items.answer: It can generate and edit panel candidates from prompts and reference images; continuity, lettering, anatomy, and rights still require review.

items.question: Should I generate a whole comic page at once?
items.answer: Generate one panel at a time so failures can be isolated and accepted panels preserved.

items.question: How do I keep a character consistent?
items.answer: Reuse approved character, location, and prop sheets as reference inputs and check every adjacent panel.

items.question: Should speech bubbles be generated in the image?
items.answer: Treat generated lettering as a draft and place final dialogue in a layout tool with editable text.

items.question: How is GPT Image 2 API cost calculated?
items.answer: Total cost includes text input, reference-image input, and image output tokens; use OpenAI’s current calculator.

items.question: What should a panel QA checklist cover?
items.answer: Identity, hands, costume, props, geography, reading order, dialogue, and print-safe margins.

items.question: Can I sell an AI-assisted comic?
items.answer: Check platform terms, reference and font rights, client or publisher rules, disclosure duties, and local law.

items.question: What is a good pilot before a full chapter?
items.answer: Use a six-panel scene with two characters, a recurring prop, a location change, target-language dialogue, and a close-up.

items.question: Can GPT Image 2 keep a character consistent across 20+ frames?
items.answer: With the right method, yes. Generate a character reference sheet — three angles of the same person — save it, and repeat a one-line identity string in every prompt. A style anchor like "black and white storyboard frame, light pencil shading" held up across all 24 frames in my test. The honest limit: past roughly frame 15, faces start to drift subtly even with references, so plan for a manual retouch or two.

items.question: What's the right workflow for building a storyboard solo?
items.answer: Plan first, generate second. Write the shot list yourself — shot number, location, action, camera angle — in a spreadsheet; the model executes a plan, it doesn't write one. Then generate an establishing frame and walk the sequence forward one edit per turn, changing a single variable at a time. That iteration is what keeps a 24-frame board coherent.

items.question: Do I need a paid Plus plan to storyboard seriously?
items.answer: For storyboarding, basically yes. Thinking mode and eight-image batch generation — the features that carry character continuity across a sequence — sit on Plus ($20/month) and above; the free tier only gets Instant mode, which handles single frames but loses that continuity advantage. Thinking mode also adds 15–30 seconds of latency per call, which is fine for drafting.

items.question: What can it still not do for storyboards?
items.answer: Three areas from my tests. Lens language is approximate — asking for "85mm, rack focus" returns something vaguely right, not accurate compression or focal falloff, so a cinematographer can't plan moves from it. Micro-action continuity between consecutive mid-motion frames drifts. And two-character dynamic scenes fall apart by frame four, with characters shifting sides. Board the key beats instead of the in-between frames.

items.question: Is it cheaper than hiring a storyboard artist?
items.answer: Almost always — and that's the honest framing. A freelancer runs roughly $10–$25 per frame at entry level and $40–$100 at professional level, so a 24-frame board costs $240–$600 at the cheap end and up to $2,500 at studio grade. GPT Image 2 is your existing $20/month subscription plus about three hours of your time.

items.question: Will GPT Image 2 replace a storyboard artist?
items.answer: Not for film or commercial production. What it replaces is not having a storyboard at all because you couldn't afford one — a different value proposition, and the one that matters most for solo operators. For a board that goes to a real production crew, the human artist is still the right answer.

items.question: Is there one best image model?
items.answer: No; compare cost per accepted asset on your recurring briefs.

items.question: Is GPT Image 2 still current?
items.answer: It remains listed, while OpenAI’s current guide points new API integrations to GPT Image 2.5 variants.

items.question: Is Nano Banana 2 the newest Google image model?
items.answer: No; Google calls it the previous-generation workhorse and recommends Nano Banana 2.1 for new projects.

items.question: How should I compare the three tools?
items.answer: Use identical prompts, references, dimensions, and acceptance criteria, then score correction time and total cost.

items.question: Which costs should be counted?
items.answer: Count inputs, outputs, edits, retries, grounding, subscription capacity, privacy needs, and human correction.

items.question: Does a leaderboard decide the best tool?
items.answer: No; a leaderboard task may not match your text, editing, brand, or production workflow.

items.question: What should I verify for commercial use?
items.answer: Verify tier, output rights, privacy, data use, reference rights, trademarks, disclosure, and local law.

items.question: When is a second image tool justified?
items.answer: Add one only when it covers a measured failure class the primary tool cannot.

items.question: Is the Grok 3 API still available?
items.answer: Not as the original model. xAI retired `grok-3` on May 15, 2026. The old slug still resolves, but requests are redirected to `grok-4.3` with reasoning effort set to `none`.

items.question: What happens if my application still sends `grok-3`?
items.answer: xAI serves the request with `grok-4.3` and bills it at Grok 4.3 rates. The automatic redirect can keep an application running, but you should migrate explicitly so configuration, evaluation records, and cost reporting identify the real model.

items.question: How much does the redirected Grok 3 request cost?
items.answer: For Grok 4.3 prompts below 200,000 tokens, xAI lists $1.25 per million input tokens, $0.20 cached input, and $2.50 output. At or above 200,000 prompt tokens, all tokens in that request use the long-context rates of $2.50, $0.40, and $5 respectively.

items.question: Which xAI model should replace Grok 3?
items.answer: Start by evaluating `grok-4.3` with `none` if you want behavior aligned with the current redirect. Consider a higher reasoning effort for complex analysis, `grok-4.7` for the current flagship, or `grok-build-0.1` for agentic coding. Use task evaluations rather than the newest model number alone.

items.question: Does Grok API include real-time X data automatically?
items.answer: No. xAI says current information requires search tools to be enabled. X Search is a separate server-side tool that can query posts, profiles, and threads and returns its own usage counts and charges.

items.question: How do I measure the real cost of a Grok API request?
items.answer: Record `usage.cost_in_usd_ticks` from each response. xAI documents this as the actual billed amount after cache discounts and including model tokens and server-side tool charges. Also retain tool-usage counts, retries, and failed outputs to calculate cost per successful job.

items.question: Can I use the OpenAI SDK with the xAI API?
items.answer: Yes. xAI's official quickstart documents OpenAI SDK usage with the xAI base URL and API key. Compatibility reduces initial integration work, but you still need regression tests for model behavior, supported fields, tools, and errors.

items.question: When is adding the xAI API not worth it?
items.answer: It is usually unnecessary when the current stack already completes the task reliably, X data is not important, there is no evaluation set, or no one will monitor tool use and spend. A raw API also does not provide file organization, approvals, scheduling, or deliverable review by itself.

items.question: What is Grok 4.6?
items.answer: Grok 4.6 is xAI's August 2026 model for coding, agentic tasks, and knowledge work. It accepts text and images, returns text, supports tool use and structured outputs, and offers four reasoning-effort settings.

items.question: How large is the Grok 4.6 context window?
items.answer: The official xAI model page lists a 500,000-token context window. That capacity is useful for large repositories and document sets, but prompts at or above 200,000 tokens enter a higher pricing tier.

items.question: How much does the Grok 4.6 API cost?
items.answer: Below 200K prompt tokens, xAI lists $2 per million input tokens, $0.50 per million cached input tokens, and $6 per million output tokens. At 200K prompt tokens or more, the listed rates are $4, $1, and $12 respectively, applied to the whole request.

items.question: Is Grok 4.6 an open-weight model?
items.answer: No. xAI provides Grok 4.6 through its API and supported products or partners, but it has not released model weights for self-hosting.

items.question: Does Grok 4.6 know current events automatically?
items.answer: No. xAI lists a February 1, 2026 knowledge cutoff and says real-time information requires server-side web or X search tools.

items.question: How did Grok 4.6 perform on benchmarks?
items.answer: At launch, xAI reported an Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score of 61 and strong agentic knowledge-work results. Benchmark versions must be checked carefully: for example, Terminal-Bench v2.1 and v3.0 results are not directly comparable.

items.question: Should a new project use Grok 4.6 or Grok 4.7?
items.answer: Grok 4.7 is xAI's newer model and is the better first candidate for a new evaluation. Grok 4.6 remains reasonable where it is already validated, where 4.7 is unavailable, or where a fixed earlier version is needed for regression testing.

items.question: How should teams evaluate Grok 4.6?
items.answer: Use representative tasks and score completion quality, tool reliability, review burden, context behavior, total token cost, and end-to-end latency. Keep the harness, permissions, reasoning setting, and retry policy equal when comparing models.

items.question: What is Grok Bot?
items.answer: Grok Bot is xAI's persistent work agent. Each Bot can use a cloud computer, sign into authorized tools, carry out multi-step jobs, and continue working after the user steps away.

items.question: Is Grok Bot the same as Grok?
items.answer: No. Grok is primarily a conversational assistant, while Grok Bot is designed to act across apps and return completed work. The products may use related models, but their execution surfaces and permissions differ.

items.question: What is @bot on X?
items.answer: @bot is an automated X account that forwards a mention or reply to the user's connected Grok Bot. X's help page says @bot does not answer the request itself.

items.question: What can Grok Bot do with X?
items.answer: After the official X plugin is connected, a Bot can search posts, read timelines, check mentions, pull trends, and manage bookmarks, subject to account permissions and product availability.

items.question: Can multiple Grok Bots work together?
items.answer: Yes. xAI supports multiple Bots running in parallel, messaging one another, and coordinating in group threads. Team Bots can also share approved context, tools, and memory across a team.

items.question: How does a Grok Bot learn a recurring workflow?
items.answer: A user can let a Bot follow a process, save it as a routine, and refine it with corrections. The routine still needs monitoring because interfaces, credentials, and source data can change.

items.question: Is Grok Bot safe to connect to work accounts?
items.answer: It can be piloted safely only with deliberate controls: dedicated or least-privilege accounts, approval gates for consequential actions, audit records, revocable credentials, and a recovery plan. A broad personal login is a poor default.

items.question: When is Grok Bot a better choice than workflow automation?
items.answer: Grok Bot is more plausible for judgment-heavy work across browser tools, especially where no clean API exists. Deterministic, rule-based processes are often easier to audit in a conventional workflow engine.

items.question: What is the best Gumloop alternative in 2026?
items.answer: There is no universal winner. Test n8n for self-hosting and custom logic, Make for managed visual SaaS automation, Relay.app for human approvals and handoffs, and Lindy for assistant-style delegation. The best choice is the one that passes your task, permission, recovery, cost, and exit tests.

items.question: Is n8n a good alternative to Gumloop?
items.answer: Yes when deployment control, custom code, direct APIs, and self-hosting matter. Include infrastructure, backups, monitoring, security maintenance, and operator time in the comparison; self-hosted software is not operationally free.

items.question: When should I choose Make instead of Gumloop?
items.answer: Choose Make when the workflow is mainly deterministic SaaS data movement and visual field mapping. Model the number of bundles and billable modules, plus external AI tokens; a single business run may consume many platform operations.

items.question: Why consider Relay.app as a Gumloop alternative?
items.answer: Relay.app documents native approvals, data requests, assigned tasks, and human path selection, with reminders and escalation. It is worth testing when accountable human decisions are part of the workflow, but each required connector action still needs verification.

items.question: How is Lindy different from Gumloop?
items.answer: Lindy emphasizes assistant-style delegation, while Gumloop can express explicit visual flows as well as agentic steps. Lindy may reduce branch design for variable tasks, but you should evaluate action permissions, confirmations, run history, and behavior when information is missing.

items.question: How do I compare automation costs across different pricing models?
items.answer: Calculate cost per accepted outcome: platform usage, hosting, model/API charges, human review and rework, and maintenance divided by accepted outputs. Compare median and p95 costs because loops, fan-out, long inputs, and retries distort averages.

items.question: How should I test a Gumloop alternative?
items.answer: Build the same bounded workflow in Gumloop and one candidate using 20–30 fixed normal and failure cases. Measure accepted-without-edit rate, false actions, runtime, normalized cost, review time, recovery time, and the effort needed to change and retest it.

items.question: Should I migrate existing Gumloop workflows?
items.answer: Only for a structural gap such as hosting, identity, approval, audit, connector action, or portability. If current flows meet acceptance, permission, recovery, and cost thresholds, optimize them before paying the risk and effort of migration.

items.question: What is Gumloop?
items.answer: Gumloop is a visual operations platform that combines deterministic flows, AI nodes, agents, triggers, interfaces, and app connections for repeatable multi-step work.

items.question: What is the difference between a Gumloop flow and an agent?
items.answer: A flow follows an explicit sequence of nodes; an agent chooses among enabled tools at runtime. An Agent Node can also run inside a deterministic flow.

items.question: Who is Gumloop best for?
items.answer: It best fits teams with recurring work, definable inputs and outputs, bounded AI judgment, available integrations, and a named owner for failures.

items.question: Is Gumloop production-ready by default?
items.answer: No. Production use still requires least-privileged credentials, validation, approvals for high-impact actions, recovery tests, monitoring, and clear ownership.

items.question: How does Gumloop pricing work in 2026?
items.answer: Gumloop’s August 2026 announcement says model tokens and compute are passed through at cost with a base 8% orchestration fee; verify the current workspace breakdown.

items.question: Whose credentials does a shared Gumloop agent use?
items.answer: It depends on the trigger and configuration. Direct Slack mentions and channel triggers can run under different identities.

items.question: How should I test Gumloop before adopting it?
items.answer: Use one bounded workflow, define accepted and forbidden outcomes, test edge cases and forced failures, then measure cost per accepted outcome.

items.question: When should I avoid Gumloop?
items.answer: Avoid it when native rules already solve the task, goals change every run, data cannot use the proposed services, failures are irreversible without review, or nobody owns operations.

items.question: Can one person work like a team with AI?
items.answer: A solo operator can adopt role boundaries, handoffs, and review gates, but AI is not an accountable employee.

items.question: What is an AI role contract?
items.answer: It defines the job, approved inputs, required output, exclusions, review criteria, and handoff.

items.question: Are AI personas enough to improve quality?
items.answer: No. Clear constraints, evidence, artifacts, and review create the operational value.

items.question: Which four AI-assisted roles can I start with?
items.answer: A practical starting loop is research, decision, production, and review.

items.question: Should every AI role share all available context?
items.answer: No. Share only approved, relevant context because flawed evidence can propagate across stages.

items.question: When should I use a workflow instead of several roles?
items.answer: Use a workflow when the sequence, inputs, and expected outputs are stable.

items.question: Which responsibilities must stay human?
items.answer: Legal responsibility, client relationships, risk tolerance, conflicts, and consequential approvals remain human.

items.question: How should I start using AI roles?
items.answer: Test two stages on one recurring deliverable and measure rework, missing evidence, and review time.

items.question: When does repeated work need an agent?
items.answer: When inputs vary and the system must choose steps or tools; fixed paths usually fit deterministic workflows.

items.question: What is a task contract?
items.answer: A definition of inputs, allowed actions, expected output, finish conditions, reviewers, and failure behavior.

items.question: How narrow should tools be?
items.answer: Each tool should have one clear purpose, explicit parameters, stable identifiers, and bounded authority.

items.question: What state should be stored?
items.answer: Only durable facts needed for future runs, with source, version, owner, and correction path.

items.question: Where should approvals go?
items.answer: Immediately before consequential external writes, sends, payments, deletion, or permission changes.

items.question: What should an evaluation set contain?
items.answer: Representative normal, edge, adversarial, and failure cases with expected facts and allowed actions.

items.question: What must be observable?
items.answer: Inputs, model and version, tool calls, evidence, state changes, approvals, cost, latency, errors, and output.

items.question: How should rollout proceed?
items.answer: Offline evaluation, shadow mode, draft-only, limited writes, then broader scope if gates pass.

items.question: What is an AI agent?
items.answer: An AI agent is a model-controlled loop that selects tools, observes results, updates its plan, and stops at an outcome or control boundary.

items.question: How is an agent different from a workflow?
items.answer: An agent selects the next step, while a workflow follows a path predetermined by code or rules.

items.question: What should I define before building an agent?
items.answer: Write a task contract covering the trigger, inputs, accepted result, forbidden actions, limits, and owner.

items.question: How should agent tools be designed?
items.answer: Keep tools narrow, typed, idempotent where possible, and separate reads from consequential writes.

items.question: What state does an agent need?
items.answer: Keep only the task state needed for the current decision and store authoritative data outside model memory.

items.question: How do I evaluate an AI agent?
items.answer: Score complete trajectories on outcome, tool correctness, constraint compliance, cost, and recovery.

items.question: What observability does an agent need?
items.answer: Trace goals, prompts, tool arguments and results, approvals, state changes, errors, cost, and final artifacts.

items.question: How should an AI agent be deployed?
items.answer: Move from offline cases to shadow mode, read-only work, reversible writes, approvals, and gradual expansion.

items.question: What counts as an AI agent in ChatGPT?
items.answer: It is a bounded, reusable workflow built from instructions, knowledge, approved apps, permissions, and a review policy.

items.question: Do I need the API to build a ChatGPT agent?
items.answer: No for workflows that stay inside ChatGPT. A custom product or unsupported integration may require platform APIs.

items.question: Should I start with a custom GPT, a plugin, or a ChatGPT Work task?
items.answer: Choose based on what must persist, which apps are needed, whether actions are required, and how long the delegation should run.

items.question: What should the agent instructions include?
items.answer: Define the goal, inputs, exclusions, output schema, allowed tools, approval points, and stop conditions.

items.question: Can a ChatGPT agent use company data?
items.answer: Only through approved files and apps, subject to workspace permissions, retention settings, and company policy.

items.question: How should I test a ChatGPT agent?
items.answer: Test normal cases plus missing data, conflicting sources, permission failures, unsafe requests, and interrupted execution.

items.question: When is human approval necessary?
items.answer: Require approval before consequential external writes, messages, purchases, deletions, or changes to production records.

items.question: How do I maintain a ChatGPT agent?
items.answer: Version its instructions and rerun a fixed evaluation set whenever the model, knowledge, apps, or permissions change.

items.question: What are the minimum parts of a DeepSeek Agent?
items.answer: You need a credential, current model, bounded tools, loop, validation, stop conditions, and logs.

items.question: Which model should a first build use?
items.answer: Start with deepseek-flash and escalate only after evaluation.

items.question: Is changing the base URL enough?
items.answer: Not for production. Feature compatibility and error behavior must be tested.

items.question: What is the agent loop?
items.answer: Send tools, receive calls, execute safely, return results, and repeat until a bounded stop.

items.question: How do I prevent infinite loops?
items.answer: Set turn, time, call, and spend limits.

items.question: How should writes be protected?
items.answer: Use least privilege, validation, approval, and idempotency keys.

items.question: What should tests include?
items.answer: Test missing evidence, malformed arguments, duplicates, outages, and denied approvals.

items.question: When should I use an existing harness?
items.answer: Use one when it already provides the sandbox, approvals, and session controls you need.

items.question: Do I need an Obsidian plugin to use an AI agent?
items.answer: No. A file-capable agent can work with an authorized vault folder directly. Use an in-vault plugin when you want AI inside Obsidian, or the official CLI for repeatable Obsidian commands.

items.question: What is the safest first AI task for a vault?
items.answer: Start read-only: ask for an inventory, a source-linked summary, or unanswered questions from one project folder. Confirm the scope before allowing a small write.

items.question: Should I give the agent access to my whole vault?
items.answer: Usually not. Grant the smallest useful project folder and exclude journals, archives, credentials, and `.obsidian/` until a task genuinely needs them.

items.question: What is an Agent Inbox?
items.answer: It is a dedicated writable folder for AI drafts. Source notes remain read-only, and a human promotes approved output into the permanent knowledge base.

items.question: When should I use Obsidian CLI instead of direct file access?
items.answer: Use CLI for structured actions such as search, note operations, daily notes, properties, or Bases. Use direct folder access when the job must combine vault notes with files outside Obsidian.

items.question: Can an AI agent break wikilinks or frontmatter?
items.answer: Yes, if it has write access. Review filenames, `[[wikilinks]]`, embeds, attachment paths, YAML keys, and value types after every small batch.

items.question: Does a local Obsidian vault mean AI processing stays local?
items.answer: No. The source files are local, but an agent or plugin may send selected content to a remote model. Check permissions, processing location, retention, and model-training terms.

items.question: How should I back up a vault before agent writes?
items.answer: Back up the entire folder, including attachments and relevant configuration, or commit a clean Git state. Sync alone is not a backup because mistakes can sync too.

items.question: What is html-anything and how does it work?
items.answer: HTML Anything is an Apache-2.0 local web app that invokes a supported coding-agent CLI already installed on your computer. It applies reusable skills, streams generated HTML into a browser preview, and exports HTML, PNG, and platform-oriented formats.

items.question: Is HTML Anything free?
items.answer: The repository has no license fee under Apache-2.0. You still pay for or consume the allowance of the connected coding agent, and you own hosting, maintenance, security review, and output QA costs.

items.question: Does HTML Anything really need no API key?
items.answer: It does not ask for a second API key because it reuses an authenticated CLI session. That does not mean the AI is free or local: usage follows the selected agent's subscription or API terms, and that CLI may send content to its cloud model provider.

items.question: Which coding agents does HTML Anything support?
items.answer: The current README lists Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Cursor Agent, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, OpenCode, Qwen Coder, Aider, and IBM Bob. The CLI must be installed, discoverable on PATH, and authenticated.

items.question: What can HTML Anything create and export?
items.answer: Its 75 skills cover nine broad surfaces including articles, decks, resumes, posters, social cards, prototypes, data reports, office documents, and Hyperframes scripts. Documented exports include standalone HTML, PNG, WeChat, X, Zhihu, and PDF for decks.

items.question: Is HTML Anything private because it is local-first?
items.answer: Not automatically. The app and files can run locally, but the chosen coding-agent CLI may transmit prompts and files to a cloud provider. You must review the agent's data terms, directory permissions, generated scripts, external assets, and export storage.

items.question: Is generated HTML safe to publish?
items.answer: Treat it as executable code. Inspect scripts, external requests, forms, copied secrets, accessibility, and responsive behavior before publishing. The sandboxed preview reduces some risk but does not prove that arbitrary generated or imported HTML is safe.

items.question: Who should use HTML Anything instead of an artifact or site builder?
items.answer: Use it when you already work with coding-agent CLIs and repeatedly produce the same visual deliverable. For one-off pages, an artifact tool is simpler; for a long-lived production website, a maintained codebase or hosted site builder is usually a better system of record.

items.question: What does “HTML is the new Markdown” mean?
items.answer: It argues that self-contained HTML can better serve some human-facing AI artifacts; it does not mean Markdown is obsolete.

items.question: Where did the phrase come from?
items.answer: It became associated with Thariq Shihipar’s article, examples, and later follow-up coverage.

items.question: What did the examples demonstrate?
items.answer: Agents can produce browser-readable plans, reviews, references, and presentations as single HTML files.

items.question: Did the article prove industry-wide adoption?
items.answer: No; it documented a proposal and examples, not universal adoption or productivity gains.

items.question: When can HTML help?
items.answer: When navigation, layout, comparison, visual status, diagrams, or interaction serve the reader’s task.

items.question: When does Markdown remain useful?
items.answer: For frequent editing, Git diffs, repositories, knowledge systems, and text pipelines.

items.question: Is self-contained HTML automatically safe?
items.answer: No; scripts, remote resources, forms, links, and embedded data still need review.

items.question: How can I test the claim?
items.answer: Generate both formats from identical approved content and measure reader task success, cost, and maintenance.

items.question: Is HTML or Markdown better for AI output?
items.answer: Neither universally; choose by audience, editing lifecycle, visual structure, and downstream reuse.

items.question: Which is easier to review in Git?
items.answer: Markdown often produces cleaner prose diffs, while generated HTML may add structural noise.

items.question: Should agent-to-agent output always be Markdown?
items.answer: No; use the validated contract the consumer expects, such as JSON, a schema, Markdown, or HTML.

items.question: Does HTML always cost more tokens?
items.answer: Styled HTML often has more markup, but measure identical content in the actual model.

items.question: When is HTML worth considering?
items.answer: For human-facing reports, reviews, prototypes, dashboards, or explanations that benefit from layout or interaction.

items.question: When is Markdown a strong default?
items.answer: For editable notes, repository documents, text pipelines, and content that moves between renderers.

items.question: Is a single HTML file portable?
items.answer: It opens in browsers, but fonts, security policy, external resources, and browser behavior still affect portability.

items.question: What is a useful hybrid workflow?
items.answer: Draft and version content in Markdown, then generate reviewed HTML for a human-facing milestone.

items.question: What is FloatIM today?
items.answer: FloatIM has a live app and product overview for agent-oriented messaging; verify every specific behavior in the current product.

items.question: Does it support group rules?
items.answer: Rule interpretation is a design goal unless the current app visibly exposes and enforces it.

items.question: Can agents take roles and coordinate?
items.answer: Multi-agent roles and coordination are concept scenarios that require a live-product pilot.

items.question: Does FloatIM pair with Floatboat?
items.answer: Desktop pairing is product direction unless current documentation shows the exact connection and permissions.

items.question: Is FloatIM local-first?
items.answer: Do not infer local data access from positioning; verify where data is processed and stored.

items.question: Does it replace team chat?
items.answer: Not automatically; compare identity, permissions, auditability, and recovery on one bounded task.

items.question: Where is the current source of truth?
items.answer: Use the live FloatIM app and the `/floatim` product overview.

items.question: How should a team pilot it?
items.answer: Test one group with known participants and review identities, allowed actions, logs, handoffs, and failure recovery.

items.question: What is Flow Mode?
items.answer: It is presented as a voice-first document experience inside Floatboat; the current build defines availability.

items.question: Is it system-wide dictation?
items.answer: No such claim is made here; its product concept centers voice and Agent-assisted edits in one document.

items.question: Can I edit while speaking?
items.answer: Verify the exact concurrent editing behavior in the current build before relying on it.

items.question: Are batch voice annotations shipped?
items.answer: They are a concept workflow unless the current build visibly supports selection anchoring and batch submission.

items.question: Can it create meeting checklists with owners?
items.answer: That is a direction scenario, not a guaranteed current capability.

items.question: Does it provide diff and one-click rollback?
items.answer: Verify history, labels, timestamps, diff, and restore controls in the current build.

items.question: Does it run on Mac and Windows?
items.answer: Platform coverage must be checked in the current release; this page does not guarantee it.

items.question: What should a pilot measure?
items.answer: Measure recognition errors, correction time, unintended edits, permission handling, recovery, and export quality.

items.question: Is Kimi K3 available in Floatboat's default picker?
items.answer: No. Floatboat has underlying capacity configuration for kimi-k3, but it is not exposed in the default picker.

items.question: What does the Kimi K3 capacity record mean?
items.answer: The runtime has a model profile and budget entry for evaluation or future routing; it is not proof of launch.

items.question: What are Kimi K3's main specifications?
items.answer: Use Moonshot's official documentation for architecture, context, modality, and benchmark claims because releases can change.

items.question: What model ID does Floatboat use?
items.answer: The confirmed underlying ID is kimi-k3. Compatibility entries do not make K3 a picker option.

items.question: Does the profile guarantee a 1M context window?
items.answer: No. A configured budget is not a user-facing guarantee; limits depend on deployment and release state.

items.question: Can I use Kimi K3 without an API key today?
items.answer: The confirmed matrix does not establish a public launch, so no-key access should not be promised.

items.question: How should teams evaluate Kimi K3?
items.answer: Test representative tasks with acceptance criteria, cost limits, and human review instead of relying on one benchmark.

items.question: What would confirm Kimi K3's Floatboat launch?
items.answer: Its appearance in the client picker or an explicit Floatboat release note.

items.question: Is Kimi K3 open weight?
items.answer: Yes. Moonshot released full weights and supporting infrastructure under the Kimi K3 License.

items.question: Is the Kimi K3 License unrestricted?
items.answer: Do not assume so; review redistribution, derivatives, hosted access, branding, and restricted-use clauses.
